metadata.title: Kindergarten pre-reading skills predict Grade 9 reading comprehension (PISA Reading) but fail to explain gender difference

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a longitudinal community sample (First Steps Study) with Kindergarten assessments (spring 2006) and a Grade 9 reading assessment aligned to PISA Reading tasks (fall 2017). The manuscript does not report the use of PISA/OECD student sampling weights or any complex survey design adjustments; instead, it reports a fixed analytic sample of 1010 adolescents with no missing data on the measures used. Because the outcome is a reading comprehension score derived from PISA Reading link items administered in a classroom setting, analysts should treat the results as conditional on this study’s sample rather than as population-representative PISA estimates. No replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is described, and the modeling is conducted with Mplus robust maximum likelihood (MLR) for skewness rather than survey-weighted estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values (PV) handling is not applicable because the Grade 9 reading outcome is analyzed as a single test score computed from the administered PISA Reading link items (total score), rather than as PV-based ILSA achievement estimates. The paper also reports that the analytic sample had no missing data in any measures used, so there is no need for PV-based multiple imputation or PV pooling. Therefore, PV handling procedures are not part of the reported analysis pipeline.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample comprised 1010 adolescents (480 girls, 530 boys) from the First Steps Study who participated in both Kindergarten assessments of pre-reading skills (spring 2006; N=1839 at Kindergarten) and the Grade 9 reading assessment using PISA Reading tasks (fall 2017). Attrition occurred over time; the authors tested whether missingness was random using Little’s MCAR test and reported small differences in Kindergarten skills between participants and non-participants in Grade 9. The Grade 9 assessment excluded small classrooms with students having special needs, and the authors note that students in special-needs education classes were not included, though children with special needs who attended regular classrooms were included. For the reported analyses, the authors state that the 1010 participants had no missing data in any measures used.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA the study leveraged Gender, Phonological awareness, Rapid naming to predict predict Grade 9 reading comprehension using PISA Reading tasks (administered i, finding that The study uses a Finnish longitudinal sample from the First Steps Study to examine whether Kindergarten pre-reading skills (age 6) predict Grade 9 reading comprehension using PISA Reading tasks (administered in fall 2017). The analytic sample included 1010 adolescents (FIN; 480 girls, 530 boys) and the outcome was a total reading comprehension score computed from PISA Reading link items administered in classrooms (60 minutes). The authors estimated multigroup and mediation path models in Mplus using robust maximum likelihood (MLR) due to skewed predictors; no machine learning algorithms were trained. Results show that Kindergarten pre-reading skills explained 27% of Grade 9 reading variance for boys and 18% for girls, with letter knowledge, rapid naming, vocabulary, and listening comprehension predicting reading depending on gender. Gender differences in PISA Reading were only partially mediated by Kindergarten skills, with indirect effects totaling about 5% of the reading variance, indicating that the adolescent gender gap emerges through pathways beyond early pre-reading measures. Limitations include attrition and the exclusion of students in special-needs education classes, and the fact that the analysis uses a single score rather than PV-based PISA achievement estimates. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse with respect to ML because the paper does not train or compare machine learning predictive models; instead, it uses multigroup and mediation path modeling to test longitudinal predictive associations and gender mediation. Consequently, ml_techniques are empty and main_findings are not populated under the schema’s ML-focused StructuredFinding requirement. The study remains empirical and reports variance explained and mediation effects, but the analytic approach is not ML-based.
